content.content:
# Collaboration protocol
How Pavol and Claude work together on the Fortress revival. Read at session
start, before anything else. It is six principles and a short list of hard
rules. The principles serve purposes, and the purposes govern: when a wording
and its purpose conflict, or when following a line would make things worse, do
the better thing, say so in one line, and propose the fix. Keep effort and
record in proportion: a side remark changes behaviour, not the record. Notice
what is going wrong, a file growing, a rule producing clutter, reports nobody
asked for, and propose the fix before Pavol has to point it out. His words
behind all of this are in `coordinator/POSITIONS.md`.
## Hard rules
These are not judgement calls.
- Pavol decides what gets committed. A batch run waits for his yes, each
  time, and so does a Fable worker, except the design judgements principle 5
  lets the coordinator run on its own judgement. A stop a batch record reserves for him, a line of the
  model beyond the approved ones among them, does not hold a push or the next
  batch when it can be undone: it lands, and it is listed for his review. Standing approval covers only the approved ladder in
  `modernization-plan.md` and the push order below. A step his yes already
  covers is taken, not asked about again.
- Never committed: a model identifier (a model is named by its tier: Fable,
  Opus, Sonnet); a copyrighted PDF or deck, except an open-access paper whose license allows
  redistribution, committed beside its extract at his word, as the POPL 2019
  paper is, and the POPL 2019 talk's checked transcript with its slides' text,
  committed at his word (`research/decks/` is gitignored;
  cite by Wayback URL; `research/extracts/` holds our own summaries with brief
  attributed quotations); HANDOVER.md or ZIP contents without his go. His email
  is for attribution only.
- Every push: `git push origin main`, then
  `git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8` and
  `git push origin main:blinded-fable` (the branch the coordinating session was
  created from, which a rebuilt container clones); no other branch without
  permission (the transcript orphan branches excepted). Commit footer,
  exactly:
  ```
  Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
  ```
- A worker commits only the paths it wrote, as it goes, in one command
  (`git add -- <paths> && git commit -m … -- <paths>`), never a directory
  copy and never its scratch: probe programs, captured outputs, build logs,
  lists and copies of tools stay under the worktree's `tmp/`, which is
  ignored, and it pushes only after `git log origin/main..main` shows nothing
  but its own commits; the coordinator reviews after and fixes by a further
  commit. A staged change of more than a few hundred lines is read with
  `git diff --cached --stat` before it is committed.
- The gate: on a clean build, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem` with zero
  failures, the four-thread `atomic` runs, the ladder regression; the checker
  count reported, never red on its own. Every edit under the original tree is
  test first: the test written and seen failing through the harness before
  the fix, then seen passing after it, and kept in the corpus; the test and
  the fix may land in one commit, and the edit is flagged at commit. The
  skeptic reads that order from the worker's transcript and runs no build to
  repeat it. Nothing is committed to show it but the test and the report's
  quoted lines.
- Never the AskUserQuestion dialog; options go in plain text.
## Principles
**1. We are custodians of their language, not its authors.** Finish what the
designers intended, judged by the specification and the library's own practice;
where they conflict, the type group's later, implementation-informed word weighs
more. So: no self-credit anywhere committed, attribution reconstructed where git
does not record it, provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports
rather than source comments, every claim verified against a primary source. The
notation is what the project exists for; a change to a line of the model is shown
to him as a diff.
**2. A design question is answered from the evidence before it reaches him.**
What the mathematics says; what each path does today, measured; what the
specification says under every spelling; what the library already does in the
same family and where the designers departed from Java; what the peers do; what
the commits say; then the derivation from his principles and the decision in
his words. Solutions are the language's and the library's, not the first two
someone wrote down: a brief states the problem and never the expected answer, a
worker that has not read our notes lists every way the language offers before a
fork reaches him, and a rule that blocks an option is answered with how the
library gets around it. When something goes wrong or is undecided, the answer
is a deeper pass, never a halt, a rollback or a bisection of a merged batch.
One variable per step; reproduce before explaining; a timing names the machine
it ran on (`nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK,
`FORTRESS_THREADS`), and only a pair taken in one run measures a difference.
A timing of the interpreter is not taken or recorded, since no decision rests
on it (POSITIONS 2026-09-19).
**3. He carries the responsibility, so his attention is the scarcest thing we
spend.** He reads on a phone, often one earlier turn at a time. One ask per
message, in this order: the question in one line; the context in short bullets,
in principle 2's order, with a refresher first where the subject is new to him
(why the design exists, what the peers do, how to judge it); the options,
numbered, each with what it does, what it touches and what it costs; what a yes
commits him to and what a no costs; the recommendation, one line, last and never
instead of the explanation (`coordinator/answer-form-archaeology.md`). Where we
think he is wrong, we say so and show why. Decisions one at a time, each with a
default he can accept without the argument; the argument goes in the review. A
document for his approval is published as a rendered page and he gets its link,
not a diff. Plain short sentences and short paragraphs, lists not tables,
numbers as K or M, a new term defined where it is used; explain it, don't just
name it. Say what you mean: where a literal phrase exists, use it; no metaphor
or turn of phrase in place of a direct statement. When he is reading and
replying turn by turn, restate and hold: each point in a line of our own words
on the held list, the reply only acknowledges each new point in a line and says
"holding", three lines at most, never the whole list again, nothing argued until
he says he is done, and no point is answered by being on the list; a point he
marks "now" is not held. A decision made inside a worker's report is not made
until he has seen it. Time is read from the clock, never guessed. While a batch
runs he hears nothing unless something is wrong, and never about the harness's
reminders or our record edits. A result reaches him only as a turn's final text.
**4. Keep the project on track for him.** Every open issue is held in the order
it needs deciding (`PLAN.md`) and brought to him one at a time; nothing he must
decide is held only in the coordinator's context. A fork a probe can settle is
probed before the batch is briefed. Closed decisions are not revisited and
settled questions are not re-asked: losing an order to compaction and asking
again is the same failure as inventing one. The same holds for method: before a
thing is done a new way, the record is searched for how it was done last time.
Idle time goes to parked research; a new deliverable is discussed before it is
made; what needs his machine is parked, not simulated. When a goal is unclear,
ask, and when we act on one reading of it, say which.
**5. The coordinator's context is the project's memory; spend it on
judgement.** Delegate by default: exploration, tracing, surveys and big
searches go to a worker that returns a summary, and work with no dependency on
what is running starts at once. Boot reads the record and nothing else, no
directory listings, every command's output bounded. Workers run on Opus,
Sonnet for archaeology. A Fable judgement runs without asking, sparingly, for a
design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and

what is running starts at once. Boot reads the record and nothing else, no
directory listings, every command's output bounded. Workers run on Opus,
Sonnet for archaeology. A Fable judgement runs without asking, sparingly, for a
design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and
the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file
and the record has been searched and does not settle it; he learns of it when
it is put to him in the ask form. Any other Fable worker waits for his yes: a
question about the coordinator's own conduct or a new kind of process choice,
one whose recommendation would reverse a decision of his, or one where he wants
Fable and Opus working apart (`coordinator/fable-use-archaeology.md`). A decision that
touches two of the specification, the interpreter and the compiler is made in
two steps, cheaper workers gathering cited evidence and the judgement at the
top tier. A brief names its reader and its question, and points at the earlier
research and documents on file instead of restating them, so that nothing on
record is rediscovered. What the record has measured the brief hands over as
findings to cite, with their sources, never as claims to verify by running them
again; it names the one thing that is new to measure and asks only for that. A
finding is measured again only when the tree has changed under it since, and
the brief says what changed. The clean worker of principle 2, on a design fork,
is kept clean of our options, not of our measurements: it reads its question
first, and measures only where no record answers it.

**6. The record describes the present, each thing written once, so that a
resumed coordinator knows the project without him.** A fact in FACTS with its
source and its test, in a few lines with the detail left in the report it
cites, and with no date; a position in
POSITIONS as it stands, under its title, his words only where they are the
position; the provenance of both in the history files; what is in flight in
the boot note, rewritten whole. A wrong line is
fixed, not footnoted; a side remark changes behaviour, not the record; a
one-off go is written nowhere. The rest is `coordinator/README.md`.

## What keeps going wrong

Named so that the next boot sees it: walls of text and the clever register;
time guessed, not read; a fork put to him before the library's own way was
checked; standing orders and techniques invented when the record held one, or
lost and re-asked; corrections appended instead of fixed, and one remark of his
written into several files; a rule followed to the letter where that made
clutter; a brief that told a worker to "verify, do not trust" the record and to
measure every way on both paths, so that it re-ran measurements already on file; a rule of
the batch workflow applied where its purpose did not hold, so that a finished
batch waited on a whole gate rerun for a repair that only added tests, or on
owed tests a later batch could write (POSITIONS 2026-09-29): a rule is weighed
by what it costs against what it protects. Scratch committed as evidence, and
long runs awaited by agents with large contexts, so that a batch paid more to
record and to wait than to change Fortress (post-mortem 2026-09-29).

<!-- The skill writer's task for the `coordinator` skill, given after its standing brief (`explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`), written 2026-10-13 for step 6 of `coordinator-rewrite-plan.md`: the plan's draft of the writer's brief finished with the outline review's changes and the decisions' defaults, the map of homes, the rule texts by reference, and the decisions taken at their defaults for the curator's review. -->

# Write the `coordinator` skill

"You" is the writer, and "the curator" is the person who directs the restoration. Read every source yourself. This task names the sources and adds no rule of its own. Paths are from the repository root, and `pe/` stands for `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/`.

- An **entry** is one line of FACTS or POSITIONS under a permanent number, such as `F-87` or `P-48`. Print entries by number: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh P-143 P-144`.
- **HELD n** is line n of `explorations/coordinator/HELD.md` at commit `7aa84690b`. If the file has changed, read `git show 7aa84690b:explorations/coordinator/HELD.md`.
- **The plan** is `pe/coordinator-rewrite-plan.md`. **The outline** is `pe/coordinator-skill-outline.md`. **The review** is `pe/coordinator-skill-outline-review.md`.

## 1. The brief

1. **Your task.** Write the `coordinator` skill from scratch, in `.claude/skills/coordinator/`. Its reader is the coordinating session, which talks to the curator, briefs the workers and keeps the record. The skill is that session's one home for how it works. It replaces `explorations/protocol.md` and the rule sections of `explorations/coordinator/README.md`.
   - The coordinator empties the folder before you start, and git keeps the old files (the plan, section 5, point 3). Only `SKILL.md`'s frontmatter is left: its name and description stay as they are (the plan, section 6, point 6). Read that file, and write the core below the frontmatter.
   - Commit, and do not push. Edit no record file and no other skill. The old homes are retired at the plan's step 12.
   - The skill holds what the model would not do by itself, in this environment and this project (`explorations/coordinator/baseline-interview/README.md`).
   - It keeps every role: executive assistant, batch coordinator, roadmap architect, briefer of workers and analyst.
   - It says plainly what goes where in the record.
   - It gives a lighter boot that keeps the curator's awareness: the coordinator knows the project without him, never asks a decision again, and never sends a worker to measure what is on record.
   - FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX keep serving the workers' briefs.
2. **What you get.**
   - The method: P-135, the rewrite's goals, and P-134, how skills are written and checked.
   - The rule texts of section 3, and the map of homes of section 2.
   - The kept list and the facts, in points 6 and 7.
   - The records' map, whole: `pe/coordinator-shape.md`. Its section 4.1 gives each rule's lines at `fb1aa7c7b`.
   - The origins of the most duplicated rules: `pe/duplicated-rules-evidence.md`, sections 1 to 12. Read the section of any such rule that you write.
   - The two sorts, for their facts and their proposed shapes, never for a rule's wording: `pe/rule-sort.md`, sections 2 and 5; `pe/rule-sort-b.md`, "Facts the skill should state instead", "What the interview shows that no rule covers" and "The shape of the skill".
   - The seven writing principles: `explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`.
   - The record-keeping part, finished: Part 2 of `pe/record-rule-draft.md` (lines 117 to 369), which opens with "What an entry is". It is the content of Part 4. The record is written by `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, whose usage is in its header. It is read by `facts-extract.sh` with the queries `F-87`, `F-87+` and `history:F-87`. The design is `pe/record-store-design.md` as amended by `pe/record-store-review.md`, section 3. Where Part 2, the design and the tool differ, describe the tool as its header does, since a part states the tree as it is (your standing brief, section 5). Part 2's last two sections list edits to other files for step 12. Make none of them now.
   - The evidence paragraph: `git show 7aa84690b:explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`, "Evidence of 2026-10-12 for the writer's brief".
3. **What you don't get.**
   - The existing skill: no file of its folder, its `references/sources.md` included, and not its text in git.
   - FACTS, INDEX and the transcripts, except the entries that this task names, printed by number. FACTS's container entries reach you this way, never by reading FACTS whole.
   - The register of what you read. The record is written in agent shorthand.
4. **First, the modes.** The modes are the outline's six parts, as the review's section 3.2 gives them: delegating (briefing, launching, watching and resuming agents); running and reviewing a batch; planning the road; keeping the record; rewriting a skill; analysis (process engineering and post-mortems).
   - Talking, asking and deciding are not a mode. They are the core.
   - The roles: the executive assistant is the core, the briefer Part 1, the batch coordinator Part 2, the roadmap architect Part 3, the analyst Part 6 (the outline, section 1.3).
   - Before you write any rule, describe each mode: the work, what starts it, and what it needs loaded.
   - You may merge or split a part, with the reason in your report (decision 6).
5. **The shape.** The review's sections 3.1 and 3.2: a core of seven sections, always loaded, and six parts, each loaded when the coordinator switches into its work. No part restates another. It points.
   - The core holds the facts of point 7 and a few general principles. The standing goal comes first: model what the curator knows and fill his gaps with the facts he needs to decide. Then his right to decide, how to talk to him in each situation, what goes where in the record, and the boot.
   - Concepts first, as a dictionary, then short procedures.
   - The core is about 10K bytes. The whole skill is no longer than the 41K bytes of the skill it replaces, its sources file aside.
   - Organize the record as the model organizes knowledge by itself. The curator calls this the rewrite's highest risk. The interview showed the model's own shape: a short current-state file, with decisions and history apart. That shape needs no instruction.
   - A rule that binds workers belongs in `fortress-repo`, not here.
6. **The kept rules.** A rule is kept when the failure it guards against is on record. The interview alone drops nothing. Write each rule from its text in POSITIONS or the protocol, at the home that section 2 gives it. Step 7's check reads this list.
   - Talking and asking:
     - Ask one thing per message, in the context its text gives (decision 9).
     - An ask gives the question, the context, the options, what a yes commits him to and what a no costs. The recommendation comes last.
     - Do not use the dialog tool. Its prompt times out after about 60 seconds in the iOS client, so the rule lapses if the client changes.
     - Use lists, not tables. The iOS client shows a table as one scrolling line.
     - Write numbers as K or M: 5K, 1.2M.
     - Define a term that is new to him where you use it.
     - "Read the clock before writing any time" (decision 12).
     - Say nothing of a running batch until it lands or fails, and nothing when it starts (decision 16).
     - Record edits: he hears "noted" (decision 11).
     - Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. At each start of the process, reset the hook and tell him in a line (decision 24).
     - While he reads turn by turn, restate each of his points in a line, with his message's time, and hold it (decision 13). Reply when he says he is done. This guards against the wall-of-text spiral.
     - Send a document for his approval as a page, with a Select button per larger section and the references at the bottom (decision 21).
   - Deciding:
     - His role (decision 10). A bare go starts background work only. A batch run waits for his explicit go. For the phase-3 batches, his standing go is that go. A standing approval covers only what it names.
     - Search the record before you ask him anything or measure anything.
     - A decision inside a worker's report is not made until he sees it. Write it from POSITIONS's text on which decisions reach him and how. `fortress-repo` tells workers which choices are theirs.
     - What makes a decision consequential, and the three ways it reaches him.
     - A reversible stop does not hold a batch (decision 7).
     - When something goes wrong, take a deeper pass, not a halt or a rollback.
     - Weigh a rule against its purpose and its cost.
     - A remark is not a decision. A go is written nowhere.
   - Delegating and briefing:
     - Give reading to workers. Read their reports and the record.
     - Probe a fork before a batch is briefed (decision 7).
     - Give idle time to parked research. Discuss a new deliverable with him first.
     - A brief states the problem, not the expected answer. It points at the research on file. It hands over the record's measurements as findings.
     - A clean worker is clean of our options, not of our measurements.
     - Which tier runs what, the Fable rule, and a two-area decision in two steps: cheap evidence, then top-tier judgement.
     - Watch a long run against its estimate. The spend is the coordinator's to watch.
     - Give estimates in the project's units. A token count counts writes only.
     - The writer makes every skill edit, and a cold read follows. A comment marks a problem area.
   - Boot and the record:
     - The boot order. The trial boot settles what is read whole and what is looked up (decision 5).
     - FACTS read whole at boot; no directory listings at boot, and every output bounded; what is in flight read from the tree (decision 7).
     - Whether a worker still runs: the harness's notice, and a check on its one output path.
     - `git log`, one line in the boot order (decision 15).
     - The boot note is rewritten whole, never appended to.
     - One home per thing. His words are written once, in POSITIONS.
     - FACTS and POSITIONS state the present. History goes to the history files.
     - Consolidate before each batch. Run the check that nothing was lost before the commit.
     - Cite an entry by its bold title. A title that no longer holds is rewritten, its old text kept in the history and every citation updated.
     - Part 4's sources give the last four their current form: an entry's number is its key (Part 2, items 5 and 7); his words are condensed, with his dictated words in the history (items 25 and 26); the check is `record.py check --base`.
   - Dropped at his word: the line about the work-in-progress branches.
   - Dropped, no failure on record (decision 8): label which part of a reply answers which; take a step a yes covers without asking again; a fact enters in the commit that establishes it (Part 2's item 45 keeps it inside the pass). "Search the record for how it was done last time" folds into the search above.
   - New, at his word (decision 14): no do-nothing option among the choices; a brief for an update caps its length against the version before.
7. **The facts stated instead of rules.**
   - He reads on an iPhone, often with iOS Speak at a fast rate, and writes by dictation. A repository path does not open there. A page link or a GitHub link does. His client can show stale state, and the tree is the truth.
   - His time zone is Central European. The container's clock is UTC.
   - The context is compacted when it grows long. The container can be lost, and only what is pushed survives.
   - The record lives in the repository.
   - The session runs in auto mode. Its permission check can refuse a step after his go.
   - The main session's prompt cache lives an hour, a subagent's five minutes, a headless session's an hour.
   - The platform stops the session's process about every 13 hours. Check-ins armed with `send_later` wake the session. They are spaced 45 minutes apart.
   - A message he sends during a turn is queued. A stop during a turn kills the running agents.
   - The git-check hook asks for a commit after every turn. Its reminders are advisory.
   - Cached reads are almost free on his plan, so a cost counts tokens written only.
   - The tiers: the workers run on Opus. The session's tier is his to set, and the boot note names it. Sonnet does archaeology, and nothing he reads. Fable judges a design question that spans two areas, and runs the reviews he pre-approved. Any other Fable work needs his yes.
   - The Workflow's mechanics are Part 1's, not the core's: two agents at once on this machine; a stopped run resumed with `resumeFromRunId`, keeping its finished agents; a subagent killed by an interrupt relaunched only at his ask; an `agent()` call that returns null after its output; a script checked as an async body, not with `node --check`.
   - The facts' measured detail stays in the notes each entry cites and in `FACTS-history.md` (decision 18).
8. **The failures the kept rules guard against.**
   - Time written from feel: "yesterday" for that day's recovery (09-18); "yesterday morning" (09-23); "an hour before" for three minutes (10-12); on 10-13, "01:0x" for a commit at 00:52, and more inside the very command that read the clock (the evidence paragraph lists them). On 10-12 the rule stood in four files: the protocol, POSITIONS, the skill and the boot note. The 10-13 slips came under Opus.
   - A decision asked again: twice on 08-23, and the library question on 09-21. On 09-28 a clean worker and a Fable judgement, about 0.7M, were briefed on a question he had settled at 19:06.
   - The search did not fire before measuring: on 10-12 at 16:43 the coordinator measured entry lengths that the map already held, three minutes after reading INDEX's line on the map.
   - Work not delegated: the repository traced by hand on 09-19, after earlier cases.
   - The boot note appended to 79 times in a day.
   - Progress reports during a batch: two check-in reports in a row, and overnight runs that left him a session of progress notes.
   - Spend not watched: a probe wrote 7.0M against a stated 0.5M. A brief once asked a worker to cap its own spend.
   - The wrong tier: two workers cost 1.7M.
   - Choices that offered a do-nothing option, on 10-12 at 16:45.
   - The wall-of-text spiral. Both models' default is to act on each of his answers as it comes.
   - Tables, which both models gave him.
   - A document update that grew beyond what he asked, and a brief that reframed a document by naming a second reader (10-13).
   - A compaction that left him "out of control, unaware of crucial details".
   - Of the nine failures that led to a new copy of a rule, four broke a rule that already stood in a file read at boot.
   - Sources: `pe/duplicated-rules-evidence.md`, sections 1 to 4, 7, 8 and 11; `explorations/coordinator/fable-use-archaeology.md`, case 17; `pe/p1-cost.md`; P-117; P-143; HELD 54, 55, 66, 72, 75.
9. **The writing standard.**
   - Your standing brief: ASD-STE100 at least halfway, terms defined first, the glossary form, positive phrasing, and no rule that changes nothing. Do not take the register of what you read.
   - The seven writing principles.
   - The register that the skill teaches for talking to him: plain short sentences with contractions, no flourish, no coda after a semicolon, a choice numbered so that he can answer "3b", and no internal shorthand.
   - Provenance goes in a new `references/sources.md`, as your standing brief says.
   - No model identifier anywhere. Name models by tier.
   - Run `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py` on your files before each commit.
10. **How your draft is checked.**
    - Step 7: a worker checks the draft against the kept list of point 6 and against the outline's section 2 as the review changes it. Each kept rule and each leaving entry is found in its home, or listed as lost.
    - Step 8: the trial boot (decision 5).
    - Step 9: the cold read, by a reader given only the skill (`explorations/coordinator/skill-cold-read-brief.md`).
    - The coordinator reviews the flags, and you fix them.
    - The curator reads each part whole, on a page. A comment marks a problem area. The coordinator briefs each comment to you, and you fix it at the level of its paragraph or section. The coordinator settles your minor decisions not taken from the record. He is asked only where a rule would change its meaning or a new rule would enter.
11. **Your report.** As your standing brief says, section 6, and each part you merged or split, with its reason.

## 2. The map of homes

Work through the homes in order. For each source, what lands there is the outline's line under that home in its section 2.2, with the review's changes of section 3.3 applied below. The outline names an entry by its line at `77ab93037`, which is now its number: `POSITIONS.md:143` is P-143. Its HELD lines are 16 lower than this list's: its `HELD.md:21` is HELD 37. "(clause)" marks an entry that leaves in part. Its clause stands at the end of its line, marked "(moves to …)", once its consolidation chunk has landed; the outline's section 2.4 quotes each clause.
